It had been sitting on your desk for three days.

The Ragged Queen.  
You’d tried not to read it.  
Swore you wouldn’t.

You’d found it in a shop that isn’t there anymore—wedged between water-damaged biographies and a copy of *Infinite Jest* with all the vowels ripped out.  
No title on the spine. Just a cracked, red leather cover and the sense that someone had already touched it too long.

You bought it.  
Then tried to give it away.  
Then tried to throw it out.  
Then, finally, you broke.

You read it in a single night.

It wasn’t even dramatic. The prose was quiet. Dense. Poetic.  
The first act was almost boring. The second? Obscenely well-written.  
By the third, you stopped noticing the page breaks.  
It never scared you. It just **felt inevitable.**

Now the book just sits there. Doesn’t ask anything. Doesn’t glow. Doesn’t bleed.

But you remember every line.

---

Your phone buzzes.

Morning.

It’s [your city]. Maybe early spring. Grey light through the blinds. Your apartment smells like coffee and heat-dust from the vents.

Outside, traffic murmurs. People walk to work. You’ve got a whole day ahead of you.

You can go anywhere.

Coffee shop.  
Library.  
Somewhere to get laid.  
Nowhere at all.

The world is still open.

But something feels… different.

It’s not loud. Not scary.  
But it’s there. In the seams. In the rhythm.

You turn your head and, for a second, you think the book is open again.  
But you didn’t touch it.

You’re sure you didn’t.

So.

What now?

Not all at once. Not aloud. But you read it. And you didn’t stop. And now? It’s too late.

The world doesn’t change immediately. It just stops behaving.

You watch someone on the train cry without tears, mouthing words you recognize from the script.

data.creator_notes:
"The Ragged Queen" is a lost theatrical manuscript, written in 1895 by a playwright named Alistair Thorne.

Its content is classified as a psychological contaminant.

Every known copy has been destroyed, suppressed, or forcibly censored by state governments, religious institutions, and private organizations. Where it is found, it is erased. Not because it offends—but because it **infects.**

The play presents itself in three acts, but no two readers ever recall the same events. Reports include hallucinations, sexual compulsion, breakdown of identity, and localized reality distortion. The final act is frequently unreadable—because the reader has already begun living it.

The Queen, it is said, does not appear on stage.

She arrives **after.**

And **you've** just read it.
